— Content strategy

Useful content. A clear reason to choose you.

Your content should help people understand what you do, decide whether it suits them, and take the next step. I turn scattered ideas and existing pages into an organized plan for useful, credible communication.

Discuss content strategy

A connected approach to content strategy

A content strategy defines who a page is for, the question it answers, and the job it does for the business. It is not simply a publishing calendar. A useful plan may recommend improving a service page, consolidating overlapping articles, or making a comparison easier to understand before commissioning more material. The aim is to create a coherent body of content that can be maintained with the time and expertise available.

When this work can help

  • The website describes services without answering customer questions.
  • Articles overlap, become outdated, or lack a clear connection to an offering.
  • Publishing decisions are driven by volume rather than useful priorities.

How I approach the work

I start with the business offering, customer questions, existing content, and the evidence available from search and analytics. Each proposed page receives a purpose, audience, outline, and next step. Subject expertise is gathered from the people who know the business, so the writing can be specific without inventing facts or relying on generic claims.

Core activities & deliverables

Content audit

Review page purpose, accuracy, duplication, structure, and maintenance needs. Recommend keeping, improving, combining, or retiring content with appropriate redirects when required.

Planning and briefs

Map topics to customer needs and appropriate page types. Prepare briefs with sources to verify, key questions, related pages, and an editorial review owner.

Copy and maintenance

Write or refine agreed pages in a consistent voice. Plan internal links, review dates, and a manageable publishing sequence so the site stays useful after launch.

Who this is for

This service suits businesses that have useful expertise but need help expressing it clearly, teams preparing a new website, and organizations with an existing content library that has become hard to manage. It also works alongside SEO, advertising, and brand positioning when those disciplines need a common message. Scope can focus on a small set of priority pages rather than an open-ended publishing commitment.

What to consider before starting

Content needs accurate source material and business review. I do not invent qualifications, case studies, testimonials, or product capabilities. Search demand and performance estimates require appropriate data; a proposed topic is not proof of traffic. AI-assisted drafting, if used, still needs fact checking, editorial judgment, and privacy-aware handling of source material.

How we assess progress

Content can be evaluated through the quality of customer inquiries, useful page journeys, organic discovery, and the role it plays in sales conversations. Not every helpful article needs an immediate conversion. Measurement should match the purpose of the page and consider whether the content is still accurate and worth maintaining.

Questions about content strategy

Do you write the content as well as plan it?+

Writing and editing can form part of an agreed scope. The business supplies factual details and reviews claims before publication.

How often should we publish?+

Choose a cadence that allows useful research, review, and maintenance. Improving a few important pages can be more valuable than publishing frequent articles without a distinct purpose.
